screens.title: Keepalived and VRRP: VIP management for HAProxy
screens.narratorSegment: In production, a single HAProxy instance is a single point of failure. In this lesson you'll learn how Keepalived uses the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol, VRRP, to float a Virtual IP between two HAProxy nodes so clients always hit the same address even when a load balancer fails. We'll walk through installing Keepalived, writing vrrp_instance blocks, adding a vrrp_script health check for HAProxy, configuring firewall rules for VRRP, and testing failover. You'll see concrete configuration snippets for a master and a backup node, learn how priority and weight change election outcomes, and run simple verifications using ip addr show and systemctl. This matters because your application availability depends on the entry point. With a VIP managed by Keepalived, back-end servers can remain unchanged while the gateway switches transparently. As you explore the chapter, think about how health checks and authentication protect the VIP, and what happens when priorities are misconfigured. After this lesson you'll be able to deploy Keepalived alongside HAProxy and validate failover in a lab environment. Consider: which failure modes should you test first to gain confidence?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical mastery
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives page focuses on applying and validating your Keepalived deployment. You will configure authentication so only authorized nodes participate in VRRP, open the VRRP protocol and VIP ports in the firewall, and run verification commands like ip addr show to confirm the VIP is assigned to the master. These skills reduce operational risk; authentication prevents malicious VRRP injections and correct firewall rules ensure advertisements are received. We will highlight two common misconceptions: first, that opening only application ports is enough; you must also allow VRRP protocol 112. Second, that identical HAProxy configs guarantee proper failover — the vrrp_instance parameters and health checks must match. screens.title: What is VRRP and how does election work?
screens.narratorSegment: VRRP stands for Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol and it is the protocol Keepalived implements to elect which node will own a Virtual IP. The basic idea is that participating nodes advertise their presence and priority; the highest-priority node becomes the master and holds the VIP. If that master fails or its effective priority drops, a backup with a higher effective priority takes over. That promotion is transparent to clients because the same IP simply appears on another node's interface. A concrete example: two HAProxy nodes participate in VRRP for virtual_router_id 51. Node A has priority 101 and Node B 100. Node A advertises more aggressively and starts as master. If Node A's health check fails, Keepalived reduces Node A's effective priority, and Node B transitions to master and configures the VIP. A frequent misconception is to treat VRRP as a simple IP move without considering health checks or authentication. In practice you must also secure VRRP advertisements with auth_pass and ensure interface and virtual_router_id match on both nodes. The core takeaway is that VRRP elects a single owner for a VIP using priority and periodic advertisements, which makes seamless failover possible.

keyIdea.title: VRRP defined
keyIdea.text: VRRP elects a master router for a VIP using periodic advertisements and priority values; the highest priority wins.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › VRRP Fundamentals
Definition

VRRP election mechanics

An election protocol where the node with the highest priority becomes master and owns the VIP.

Key signals
  • VRRP advertisements sent periodically
  • Priority values determine election winner
  • Health checks can add weight or reduce effective priority
Concrete example
Two nodes, virtual_router_id 51, priorities 101 and 100. Master is 101; if it fails, 100 becomes master and configures the VIP.
Common misconception
Thinking VRRP alone solves application availability; you still need backend health and proper HAProxy config.
Annotated flow
1
Start VRRP
Nodes send advertisements at advert_int intervals.
2
Election
Highest priority becomes MASTER and assigns the VIP to its interface.
3
Health change
vrrp_script failures reduce effective priority and can trigger failover.
4
Failover
A backup becomes master and configures the VIP; clients keep using the same IP.

screens.title: Installing Keepalived and enabling the service
screens.narratorSegment: Installation is straightforward but must be done on every HAProxy node. The chapter provides the single package command for RHEL-based systems: install keepalived with the package manager. After installation enable the service so it starts on boot and check status to confirm it is running. A concrete sequence is: sudo dnf install -y keepalived, then sudo systemctl enable --now keepalived, and finally sudo systemctl status keepalived. Running these commands on both master and backup ensures both can participate in VRRP. A common misstep is to install on only one node; Keepalived needs peers to participate in elections. Another mistake is to forget to open the firewall for VRRP protocol 112 — even a correctly installed service won't function if advertisements are blocked. After enabling the service, verify networking state with ip addr show eth0 or your interface to confirm the VIP appears on the current master. These simple operational checks are the fastest way to validate your installation before moving to configuration of vrrp_instance blocks and health checks. Installing Keepalived and enabling the service means install keepalived on both nodes, enable the service, and verify it's running before configuring vrrp instances.. In practical terms, commands to install, enable, and check keepalived on rhel/centos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Install & Start
Process

Install and enable Keepalived

Follow these exact commands to prepare each HAProxy node.

sudo dnf install -y keepalived
sudo systemctl enable --now keepalived
sudo systemctl status keepalived
Why enable now
Enabling the service immediately ensures Keepalived participates in the VRRP elections and survives reboots.
Check
Use ip addr show <interface> to confirm the VIP appears after Keepalived becomes master.
Common mistakes
  • Installing only on one node — both must run Keepalived.
  • Not opening VRRP protocol 112 in the firewall.
  • Forgetting to match virtual_router_id and auth on all nodes.
Key Takeaway

Install and start Keepalived on every HAProxy node and verify service and network state before configuring VRRP instances.

screens.title: keepalived.conf: vrrp_instance fields you must know
screens.narratorSegment: The vrrp_instance block in keepalived. conf is where you declare the VIP, election parameters, and any tracking scripts. Important fields are state which sets the node's initial role, interface which determines where the VIP will be placed, virtual_router_id which must match across participants for the same VIP, and priority which determines who becomes master. advert_int configures the heartbeat frequency. Authentication blocks secure the VRRP packets so only nodes sharing the auth_pass can influence the election. For example, the master configuration uses state MASTER and priority 101 while the backup uses state BACKUP and priority 100; both use virtual_router_id 51 and identical auth_pass. If advert_int is too long the detection of failures becomes slower; if too short, network chatter increases. One misconception is to think priority alone controls failover speed — advert_int and health check intervals also change responsiveness. Ensure the interface name matches the actual network device; an interface mismatch prevents the VIP from appearing. The key operational rule: virtual_router_id, auth_pass, and interface must align across nodes to ensure predictable failover behavior. keepalived.conf: vrrp_instance fields you must know means match virtual_router_id, auth_pass, and interface across nodes; use priority and advert_int to tune election behavior.. keyIdea.text: Match virtual_router_id, auth_pass, and interface across nodes; use priority and advert_int to tune election behavior.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › vrrp_instance Fields

Essential fields

state
Initial role: MASTER or BACKUP. It is a starting point; election rules decide final master.
interface
Network device used for VRRP advertisements and VIP assignment.
virtual_router_id
Unique ID for the VRRP group. Must be identical on all participants for this VIP.
priority & advert_int
Priority elects master; advert_int controls heartbeat frequency and failover responsiveness.

Configuration checklist

Consistency
virtual_router_id, auth_pass, and interface must match between master and backup.
Tuning
Lower advert_int increases detection speed but raises network traffic; tune for your environment.
Misconfiguration risk
An interface mismatch or ID mismatch prevents the VIP group from forming correctly.

screens.title: vrrp_script: health checks and weight
screens.narratorSegment: vrrp_script allows Keepalived to run an external script or command periodically and adjust node priority based on success or failure. Typical use is to check whether HAProxy is active by running systemctl is-active haproxy. In the example, the script runs every two seconds and applies a weight of 20 when the check passes. That weight raises the node's effective priority, making it more likely to remain master. If the script fails, the weight is not applied and the node's effective priority drops. If this makes it lower than the backup, that backup takes over and configures the VIP. This mechanism ties service health directly to master selection, preventing a node that has a downed HAProxy from serving the VIP while it cannot forward traffic. A common misunderstanding is thinking vrrp_script restarts services; it only changes priority and can influence failover. Always test your check independently to ensure it returns the expected exit codes and interval values are tuned so false positives or network delays don't cause unnecessary flapping. vrrp_script: health checks and weight means vrrp_script runs checks that add or remove weight from priority; failing checks reduce priority and can trigger failover.. keyIdea.text: vrrp_script runs checks that add or remove weight from priority; failing checks reduce priority and can trigger failover.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › vrrp_script Health Checks

How checks influence election

Checks run at interval and weight affects effective priority.

Example check
vrrp_script chk_haproxy {
    script "/usr/bin/systemctl is-active haproxy"
    interval 2
    weight 20
}
Concrete effect
If the script returns success the node gains 20 points, helping it keep master. If it fails, those points are removed and failover can occur.

Operational tips

  • Test the script independently to ensure exit codes are predictable.
  • Tune interval to balance detection speed and false positives.
  • Prefer simple checks that reflect true service readiness.
Key Takeaway

Use vrrp_script to link service health to VRRP elections; failing checks lower priority and trigger failover.

keyIdea.title: Master config
keyIdea.text: Master configuration sets higher priority, declares the VIP, and ties a vrrp_script to priority adjustments so HAProxy health affects mastership.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Master Configuration

Master (example)

# /etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf on HAProxy-Master (e.g., 192.168.1.50)
global_defs {
    router_id LVS_DEVEL
}

vrrp_script chk_haproxy {
    script "/usr/bin/systemctl is-active haproxy"
    interval 2
    weight 20
}

vrrp_instance VI_1 {
    state MASTER
    interface eth0
    virtual_router_id 51
    priority 101
    advert_int 1
    authentication {
        auth_type PASS
        auth_pass mysecretpassword
    }
    virtual_ipaddress {
        192.168.1.200/24 dev eth0 label eth0:0
    }
    track_script {
        chk_haproxy
    }
}

Notes and checks

  • Change eth0 and 192.168.1.200 to match your lab network.
  • Verify auth_pass matches the backup to avoid authentication mismatch.
  • Test the script manually to ensure it returns expected exit codes.
Pro tip

Keep the health check simple and quick. systemctl checks are reliable for service presence but consider user checks for readiness if needed.

screens.title: Backup node keepalived.conf example
screens.narratorSegment: The backup configuration mirrors the master's keepalived. conf but sets state BACKUP and a lower priority. The chapter shows a Backup with router_id LVS_BACKUP and priority 100; everything else — virtual_router_id, interface, authentication, virtual_ipaddress, and the chk_haproxy script — must match. The symmetry ensures both nodes are eligible to own the VIP, and the lower priority means the backup will yield to the master while remaining ready to take over. Important operational notes: if you set identical priorities the node that starts first becomes master, which is less predictable and often undesirable. Also confirm the network interface exists; a typographical error in interface name is a common cause of VIP not appearing. After starting both nodes, check ip addr show on each; the VIP should appear on the master only. When the master loses health, you will observe the VIP on the backup. If preemption is enabled by default, a recovered higher-priority node will reclaim the VIP, so decide whether you want that behavior or prefer nopreempt for manual failback control. keyIdea.text: Backup mirrors master but with lower priority; keep IDs, auth, and interface identical to ensure correct failover behavior.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Backup Configuration

Backup (example)

# /etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf on HAProxy-Backup (e.g., 192.168.1.51)
global_defs {
    router_id LVS_BACKUP
}

vrrp_script chk_haproxy {
    script "/usr/bin/systemctl is-active haproxy"
    interval 2
    weight 20
}

vrrp_instance VI_1 {
    state BACKUP
    interface eth0
    virtual_router_id 51
    priority 100
    advert_int 1
    authentication {
        auth_type PASS
        auth_pass mysecretpassword
    }
    virtual_ipaddress {
        192.168.1.200/24 dev eth0 label eth0:0
    }
    track_script {
        chk_haproxy
    }
}

Differences to note

  • State is BACKUP and priority is lower (100) than master (101).
  • Other fields must be identical: virtual_router_id, auth_pass, interface, and scripts.
  • Decide on preemption behavior based on operational needs: default preempt reclaims VIP on recovery.
Key Takeaway

Backup nodes must mirror the master's configuration except for state and priority to allow predictable failover.

screens.title: Firewall and networking requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Keepalived depends on VRRP protocol traffic and correct network configuration. You must open protocol 112 on each Keepalived node and ensure application ports for the VIP, such as 80 and 443, are permitted. Commands in the chapter show firewall-cmd usage: sudo firewall-cmd --add-protocol=vrrp --permanent and sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=80/tcp --permanent followed by reload. Without protocol 112, advertisements are blocked and the VRRP group cannot form, which leads to failed or unpredictable failover. Also ensure the VIP's subnet matches the interface and routing; the VIP should be assigned to the same interface clients use to reach the service. A common error is adding ports on only one node or opening only application ports but not VRRP; both nodes must accept protocol 112. After changing firewall rules, reload the firewall and check connectivity. If you still see problems, confirm ip addr show lists the VIP only on the master, and use tcpdump or system logs if advertisements appear missing. Correct firewall and interface configuration ensures advertisements are exchanged and the VIP is reachable from clients. screens.title: Testing failover scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: Testing failover is essential to validate your Keepalived design. The chapter outlines three common scenarios to test. First, a service failure: stop HAProxy on the master with sudo systemctl stop haproxy and observe that the vrrp_script fails, priority drops, and the backup takes over the VIP. Third, a full node failure or reboot: reboot the master and watch the VIP move to the backup during downtime. After recovery, if default preemption is enabled the master will reclaim the VIP once its health checks pass. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter lists several common mistakes that frequently cause Keepalived to behave incorrectly. First, virtual_router_id mismatch: if the VRRP ID differs across nodes they won't join the same group. Second, authentication mismatch in auth_pass prevents legitimate advertisements from being accepted, silently blocking failover. Third, interface mismatch where the interface name in keepalived. conf doesn't exist or is wrong, preventing VIP assignment. Fourth, priority misconfiguration where equal priorities lead to unpredictable master selection. Fifth, health check script errors: if the vrrp_script is miswritten or returns unexpected codes, it can cause incorrect failovers. Sixth, firewall misconfiguration where protocol 112 or VIP ports are blocked. To avoid these issues, validate every field, test scripts independently, and run firewall commands on both nodes. Keep a small test harness: check ip addr, systemctl status, and simulate failovers in maintenance windows. The simplest safety practice is to standardize configuration across nodes and script verification steps so human error is minimized. fullNarratorScript:
In production, a single HAProxy instance is a single point of failure. In this lesson you'll learn how Keepalived uses the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol, VRRP, to float a Virtual IP between two HAProxy nodes so clients always hit the same address even when a load balancer fails. We'll walk through installing Keepalived, writing vrrp_instance blocks, adding a vrrp_script health check for HAProxy, configuring firewall rules for VRRP, and testing failover. You'll see concrete configuration snippets for a master and a backup node, learn how priority and weight change election outcomes, and run simple verifications using ip addr show and systemctl. This matters because your application availability depends on the entry point. With a VIP managed by Keepalived, back-end servers can remain unchanged while the gateway switches transparently. As you explore the chapter, think about how health checks and authentication protect the VIP, and what happens when priorities are misconfigured. After this lesson you'll be able to deploy Keepalived alongside HAProxy and validate failover in a lab environment. Consider: which failure modes should you test first to gain confidence?

By the end of the first objectives block you'll be able to describe the role of Keepalived and VRRP in protecting HAProxy, install Keepalived on both nodes, and reason about why a floating VIP removes the load balancer as a single point of failure. You will also be able to write a working keepalived. conf vrrp_instance and explain the key parameters that determine master election. I will show a concrete installation command and a configuration excerpt to make this tangible. Understanding these basics matters because the VIP is the public-facing address that preserves client connectivity. A common misconception is to think that backend health alone is enough; without VIP failover, a failed load balancer still takes the service offline. This block sets the foundation so that when you implement health checks and failover testing you'll know what each configuration line does and how the election outcome is determined.

This second objectives page focuses on applying and validating your Keepalived deployment. You will configure authentication so only authorized nodes participate in VRRP, open the VRRP protocol and VIP ports in the firewall, and run verification commands like ip addr show to confirm the VIP is assigned to the master. These skills reduce operational risk; authentication prevents malicious VRRP injections and correct firewall rules ensure advertisements are received. We will highlight two common misconceptions: first, that opening only application ports is enough; you must also allow VRRP protocol 112. Second, that identical HAProxy configs guarantee proper failover — the vrrp_instance parameters and health checks must match. By mastering these tasks you'll be prepared to run the hands-on lab, perform a controlled failover, and interpret behavior during both service and node failures. Think ahead about how you'll test preemption and whether you want default preempt behavior in your environment.

VRRP stands for Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol and it is the protocol Keepalived implements to elect which node will own a Virtual IP. The basic idea is that participating nodes advertise their presence and priority; the highest-priority node becomes the master and holds the VIP. If that master fails or its effective priority drops, a backup with a higher effective priority takes over. That promotion is transparent to clients because the same IP simply appears on another node's interface. A concrete example: two HAProxy nodes participate in VRRP for virtual_router_id 51. Node A has priority 101 and Node B 100. Node A advertises more aggressively and starts as master. If Node A's health check fails, Keepalived reduces Node A's effective priority, and Node B transitions to master and configures the VIP. A frequent misconception is to treat VRRP as a simple IP move without considering health checks or authentication. In practice you must also secure VRRP advertisements with auth_pass and ensure interface and virtual_router_id match on both nodes. The core takeaway is that VRRP elects a single owner for a VIP using priority and periodic advertisements, which makes seamless failover possible.

Installation is straightforward but must be done on every HAProxy node. The chapter provides the single package command for RHEL-based systems: install keepalived with the package manager. After installation enable the service so it starts on boot and check status to confirm it is running. A concrete sequence is: sudo dnf install -y keepalived, then sudo systemctl enable --now keepalived, and finally sudo systemctl status keepalived. Running these commands on both master and backup ensures both can participate in VRRP. A common misstep is to install on only one node; Keepalived needs peers to participate in elections. Another mistake is to forget to open the firewall for VRRP protocol 112 — even a correctly installed service won't function if advertisements are blocked. After enabling the service, verify networking state with ip addr show eth0 or your interface to confirm the VIP appears on the current master. These simple operational checks are the fastest way to validate your installation before moving to configuration of vrrp_instance blocks and health checks. Installing Keepalived and enabling the service means install keepalived on both nodes, enable the service, and verify it's running before configuring vrrp instances.. In practical terms, commands to install, enable, and check keepalived on rhel/centos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The vrrp_instance block in keepalived. conf is where you declare the VIP, election parameters, and any tracking scripts. Important fields are state which sets the node's initial role, interface which determines where the VIP will be placed, virtual_router_id which must match across participants for the same VIP, and priority which determines who becomes master. advert_int configures the heartbeat frequency. Authentication blocks secure the VRRP packets so only nodes sharing the auth_pass can influence the election. For example, the master configuration uses state MASTER and priority 101 while the backup uses state BACKUP and priority 100; both use virtual_router_id 51 and identical auth_pass. If advert_int is too long the detection of failures becomes slower; if too short, network chatter increases. One misconception is to think priority alone controls failover speed — advert_int and health check intervals also change responsiveness. vrrp_script allows Keepalived to run an external script or command periodically and adjust node priority based on success or failure. Typical use is to check whether HAProxy is active by running systemctl is-active haproxy. In the example, the script runs every two seconds and applies a weight of 20 when the check passes. That weight raises the node's effective priority, making it more likely to remain master. If the script fails, the weight is not applied and the node's effective priority drops. If this makes it lower than the backup, that backup takes over and configures the VIP. This mechanism ties service health directly to master selection, preventing a node that has a downed HAProxy from serving the VIP while it cannot forward traffic. A common misunderstanding is thinking vrrp_script restarts services; it only changes priority and can influence failover. Keepalived depends on VRRP protocol traffic and correct network configuration. You must open protocol 112 on each Keepalived node and ensure application ports for the VIP, such as 80 and 443, are permitted. Testing failover is essential to validate your Keepalived design. The chapter outlines three common scenarios to test. First, a service failure: stop HAProxy on the master with sudo systemctl stop haproxy and observe that the vrrp_script fails, priority drops, and the backup takes over the VIP. Second, a Keepalived process failure: stop keepalived on the master with sudo systemctl stop keepalived; the backup should immediately assume the VIP because the master stops advertising. Third, a full node failure or reboot: reboot the master and watch the VIP move to the backup during downtime. After recovery, if default preemption is enabled the master will reclaim the VIP once its health checks pass. The chapter lists several common mistakes that frequently cause Keepalived to behave incorrectly. First, virtual_router_id mismatch: if the VRRP ID differs across nodes they won't join the same group. Second, authentication mismatch in auth_pass prevents legitimate advertisements from being accepted, silently blocking failover. Third, interface mismatch where the interface name in keepalived. conf doesn't exist or is wrong, preventing VIP assignment. Fourth, priority misconfiguration where equal priorities lead to unpredictable master selection. Fifth, health check script errors: if the vrrp_script is miswritten or returns unexpected codes, it can cause incorrect failovers. Sixth, firewall misconfiguration where protocol 112 or VIP ports are blocked. To avoid these issues, validate every field, test scripts independently, and run firewall commands on both nodes. Keepalived provides high availability for services like HAProxy by managing a floating Virtual IP and running VRRP elections. VRRP elects a master using priority and periodic advertisements; the master configures the VIP and backups stand ready. vrrp_script links service health to elections by adjusting priority via weight so a failing service causes failover. Important operational items are consistent virtual_router_id and auth_pass across nodes, using the correct interface for the VIP, opening VRRP protocol 112 and application ports, and verifying VIP assignment with ip addr show. Testing service stop, Keepalived stop, and node reboot scenarios demonstrates real behavior and informs tuning of advert_int and script intervals. Before you begin the hands-on lab keep these compact reminders in mind: ensure both nodes run Keepalived and have matching virtual_router_id and authentication, verify interface names and VIP subnets, and open VRRP protocol 112 plus the VIP's service ports on both nodes. Use vrrp_script to tie HAProxy health to priority so a failing load balancer triggers failover, and test three scenarios—service stop, keepalived stop, and node reboot—to observe behavior. Watch ip addr show on both nodes and run a continuous curl to the VIP from a client to verify client continuity. Finally, be deliberate about preemption behavior: default preempt causes a recovered higher-priority node to reclaim the VIP, but nopreempt preserves the current master until manually changed. These checkpoints reduce common errors and help you achieve predictable VIP failover in production-like labs.
